extracted.intended_audience: startup founders, executives, and early-stage PR/communications teams
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and practical rules for startup leaders and comms teams on how to handle media outreach, interviews, messaging, and internal communications to avoid common PR mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: MISTAKE #1: FAKING IT
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t ‘fake it’ publicly — exaggerating or stretching the truth to appear further along or more visionary can lead to reputational and legal risk (example: Theranos) and generally backfires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overclaiming traction, partnerships, or capabilities. Recognize subtle ways teams 'fake it' and the long-term dangers of hype; prioritize authenticity over appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect it back
rubrics_metrics.description: Stay grounded in your company’s mission, vision, and values; ensure public statements map back to what the company stands for and what the team is passionate about.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a few lines that center messaging; use values to guide hiring, rewards, business decisions, and press talking points so external statements are consistent with internal reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be deliberate about how and what you speak about
rubrics_metrics.description: Be intentional as a spokesperson about topics you choose to speak on and the style you adopt — focus on areas you can authentically speak to rather than trying to be who you’re not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask 'Who are you to your core?' and avoid performing traits (e.g., forced humor) that feel inauthentic. Know when and how you show up best and design appearances around that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use an audit to get real feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicit candid feedback from your team or trusted colleagues about where you 'crush it' and where you fall down to understand authentic strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give permission for honesty; use an audit as a cheap, actionable exercise to surface blind spots before you speak publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop an executive brand profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a concise profile for key spokespeople (three to four topics/platforms) that maps authentic strengths to targeted media opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews to identify authentic topics, then restrict outward pitching and speaking opportunities to those themes so effort is focused and opportunities that don't fit are filtered out.

rubrics_metrics.name: MISTAKE #2: OVERSHARING
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying too much — whether from ego, nerves, or a desire to be understood — often creates more problems than it solves. Avoid unnecessary transparency in interviews and media interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize motives to over-share and be selective about when to participate in interviews; sometimes silence or passing on an interview is the smarter move.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t fill up the silence
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters use silence as a tactic to bait spokespeople into saying more; reflexively filling pauses typically leads to more damaging or off-message comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice being comfortable with silence after delivering your message; avoid 'winging it' or speaking to cover awkwardness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your message, deliver it, and then put a period on it
rubrics_metrics.description: Be concise: identify the message you want to convey, deliver it cleanly, and stop talking rather than keep adding qualifiers or anecdotes that dilute the point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the interview as a job with clear objectives; respect journalists’ roles but remember you’re not on the same team — stick to your goals and avoid over-explaining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define rules of engagement with reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use media conventions like 'off the record', 'on background', or 'exclusive' strategically to shape how information is used and protect sensitive context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage handshake agreements when you have established relationships to provide context without creating quotable material; be explicit about terms where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stick to the truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not embellish facts — reporters will check details and exaggerations can damage relationships and future opportunities (and risk partnerships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer accuracy and simplicity; truthful messages are easier to remember and defend. Avoid overstating partnerships, integrations, or traction.

rubrics_metrics.name: MISTAKE #3: ANSWERING THE QUESTIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: The mistake is treating an interview as a Q&A where you simply answer the reporter's questions; instead the objective should be to deliver your pre-defined messages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control what you can (your responses and tone) and use interview techniques to steer conversation toward your points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit yourself to your top messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the top three messages you want to convey in any interview and anchor answers to those, rather than trying to cover too many topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distill announcements or narratives into a few key points and use 'color' and examples underneath those pillars; too many messages dilute impact and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for the tough ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a list of the five worst questions you could be asked (business model, competition, exit plans, skeletons in closet) and prepare outlines for handling them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do homework on the journalist’s past work and style; be honest about vulnerabilities and rehearse responses as if the toughest questions will come up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Block and bridge technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard comms tactic: briefly acknowledge/answer the reporter's question (block) and then transition (bridge) to the message you want to deliver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use starter bridge phrases such as 'That’s an interesting observation...but the heart of the matter is really…' or 'You raise a good point about a key issue…How we like to think about XYZ is…' Practice smooth pivots that feel natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the negative (don’t repeat the negative)
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronted with loaded or negative framing, don’t restate the negative in your reply (avoid 'but' or repeating the phrase); instead redirect to solutions or positive framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use redirect phrases like 'Another way of thinking about this is…', 'I think what you’re really asking is…', or 'That speaks to a bigger point about…' Focus on solutions rather than re-echoing the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t be intentionally obtuse
rubrics_metrics.description: While you should steer interviews, avoid being obviously evasive or refusing to answer — that can create viral clips and damage credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance message discipline with respectful give-and-take; be cooperative but not a puppet, and avoid creating the impression you’re dodging responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: MISTAKE #4: FORGETTING YOUR NUMBER ONE (EMPLOYEES)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat employees as your primary audience: internal comms are critical and often overlooked, yet they shape external credibility and storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test messaging internally first — if employees don’t buy it, external audiences probably won’t either. Use employees as a reality check and ambassadors when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in internal comms expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Hire or assign specialists who understand employee communications rather than treating it as an afterthought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dedicated internal comms roles help cascade messages through leaders and mid-level managers, improving consistency and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide leader-facing summaries (things to know/do/share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give leaders concise, actionable communications (e.g., weekly leader emails broken into 'things to know, things to do, things to share') so they can cascade messages effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equip expensive leadership time with 'cliff notes' and tools that make it easy for them to communicate clearly and timely to their teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find micro-moments to connect
rubrics_metrics.description: Create small-group or informal touchpoints (e.g., weekly coffee breaks with the CEO for six people) to give employees face time and build two-way communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use micro-moments to surface employee concerns, test ideas, and let leaders hear diverse perspectives beyond large town halls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go beyond infrequent all-hands
rubrics_metrics.description: Monthly all-hands or town halls are not enough; employees need more frequent and varied channels of connection to feel engaged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a cadence of communications — frequent, authentic, and two-way — rather than relying on occasional large meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABOVE ALL, PUT IN THE WORK
rubrics_metrics.description: Communications success requires ongoing effort: cultivate media networks, practice speaking to reporters, and be humble about continual improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether hiring a comms lead or DIY-ing it, invest time learning how to talk to the press; accept you likely need practice and that sustained effort pays off.
